🧭 Spermatocele/Epididymal Cyst
Benign epididymal-region cystic lesions are common causes of a painless palpable scrotal mass. A spermatocele contains spermatozoa and debris, whereas an epididymal cyst contains simple serous or lymphatic fluid; routine imaging often cannot reliably separate them.
Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis. Core Radiology, 2nd ed., GU Scrotum and testicle pp. 285 and 291-292; RadPrimer and STATdx master source package.

📖 Summary
  • Spermatocele: cystic dilation or retention cyst of the epididymal/efferent duct system containing spermatozoa, usually in the epididymal head but potentially elsewhere.
  • Epididymal cyst: epithelial-lined cyst containing simple serous or lymphatic fluid; it may occur anywhere in the epididymis.
  • Ultrasound often cannot reliably distinguish a simple epididymal cyst from a spermatocele; the distinction is usually clinically irrelevant.

🔍 Key Imaging Findings
Ultrasound
  • Simple epididymal cyst: circumscribed, anechoic, thin-walled, and avascular.
  • Spermatocele: simple or complex cystic mass that may be multiseptated and contain debris or diffuse low-level echoes.
  • Falling snow sign: mobile punctate low-level echoes moved by Doppler-related acoustic streaming, favoring spermatocele.
  • Dilated rete testis in the mediastinum testis may accompany a spermatocele.
  • For a palpable complaint, scan directly over the area of concern.

CT
  • When encountered, CT may show a well-circumscribed uni- or multilocular cystic lesion near the superior pole of the testis.

MR Imaging
  • Low T1 signal, high T2 signal, and no enhancement; septations may be present.

⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Hydrocele surrounds the testis rather than forming a focal epididymal cyst.
  • Hematocele is associated with trauma and complex tunica vaginalis fluid containing clot or fibrin strands.
  • Pyocele occurs with epididymoorchitis and complex tunica vaginalis fluid, often with a hyperemic rim.
  • Tunica albuginea cyst is usually a small simple cyst along the testicular surface.
  • Abscess is considered with recent epididymitis and persistent hyperemia; inguinal hernia changes with Valsalva and shows bowel signature or fat.

🧬 Clinical / Path / Mechanism
  • Etiology is often unknown but may follow epididymitis, trauma, vasectomy, or obstruction of the efferent ductal system.
  • Suspended spermatozoa, lymphocytes, and debris account for internal low-level echoes and mobile particulate material.
  • Reported size ranges from roughly 3 mm to 10 cm.

📌 Pearls / Pitfalls
  • A cystic extratesticular lesion without vascularized soft tissue is almost always benign and should not be treated as a neoplasm.
  • Large lesions may displace the testis and may require a curved-array transducer for complete visualization.
  • Most lesions are observed when asymptomatic; spermatocelectomy is reserved for lesions large or symptomatic enough to cause discomfort. RadPrimer also notes alcohol aspiration/sclerotherapy in selected cases.

⭐ Super Summary
  • Think spermatocele when an epididymal-head cyst contains mobile low-level echoes, falling snow, septations, debris, or associated rete testis dilation; accept that a simple epididymal cyst may be indistinguishable by imaging.

column11: Why can a spermatocele show the falling snow sign on color Doppler ultrasound?
column12: The rete testis and efferent/epididymal ducts normally transport and concentrate sperm. Obstruction or scarring can dilate the ductal system and retain spermatozoa, lymphocytes, and debris within a cystic space. These suspended particles create low-level echoes. Doppler-related acoustic radiation force and acoustic streaming move the particles in real time, producing the falling snow appearance. The mobility of the echoes and absence of vascularized soft tissue favor particulate cyst contents rather than a solid neoplasm.

column11: How can epididymal outflow obstruction link a spermatocele to tubular ectasia of the rete testis?
column12: The rete testis drains through the efferent ductules into the epididymis. Obstruction or dilation of the efferent epididymal system can create a spermatocele while increasing upstream pressure in the rete, producing multiple tiny dilated tubules in the mediastinum testis. On imaging, a focal epididymal cystic lesion plus associated dilated rete testis supports spermatocele; tubular ectasia itself remains centered intratesticularly at the mediastinum testis.
